title-group.article-title: Datopotamab deruxtecan in Chinese patients with heavily pretreated advanced or metastatic triple-negative breast cancer in the phase I/II TROPION-PanTumor02 study

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Despite recent improvements in treatment, outcomes for patients with pretreated, advanced triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) remain poor. We present results from the phase I/II TROPION-PanTumor02 study of datopotamab deruxtecan (Dato-DXd), an antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) comprised of a humanised anti-trophoblast cell surface antigen 2 (TROP2) monoclonal antibody conjugated to a potent topoisomerase I (Topo-I) inhibitor, in Chinese patients with pretreated, advanced TNBC.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: Patients received Dato-DXd 6 mg/kg intravenously every 3 weeks until radiological progression or another discontinuation criterion was met. The primary endpoint was objective response rate (ORR) per independent central review (ICR); secondary endpoints included progression-free survival (PFS), overall survival (OS), and safety.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: At data cutoff (6 May 2024), 79 patients had received treatment. Median age was 50.0 years (range, 33–73 years) and 74 (93.7%) patients had metastatic disease; 33 (41.8%) had liver metastases. Patients had received a median of 3 (range, 2‒8) prior lines of chemotherapy for advanced disease [≥5 lines, n=21 (26.6%)]. ORR by ICR was 33.8% [95% confidence interval (CI): 23.4–45.4%]. Median PFS and OS were 5.3 months (95% CI: 4.2–6.9) and 13.5 months [95% CI: 10.7–not calculable (NC)], respectively. The most common treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) were stomatitis (49.4%) and nausea (43.0%). Twenty-five patients (31.6%) experienced grade ≥ III TRAEs. Adjudicated drug-related interstitial lung disease (ILD) was reported in 1 patient (grade II).

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Dato-DXd monotherapy demonstrated clinical activity and manageable safety in Chinese patients with heavily pretreated, advanced TNBC. Phase III studies of Dato-DXd alone or in combination in early-stage and advanced TNBC are ongoing.

sec.title: Key findings
sec.p: • The trophoblast cell surface antigen 2 (TROP2)-directed antibody-drug conjugate (ADC), datopotamab deruxtecan (Dato-DXd), demonstrated clinical activity and manageable safety in Chinese patients with heavily pretreated, advanced triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC).

• The objective response rate (primary endpoint) was 33.8% [95% confidence interval (CI): 23.4–45.4%]; median progression-free survival and overall survival were 5.3 months (95% CI: 4.2–6.9) and 13.5 months (95% CI: 10.7–not calculable), respectively. No new safety signals were identified.

sec.title: What is known and what is new?
sec.p: • TROP2 is expressed in various solid tumours, including breast cancer, and is associated with poor prognosis.

• Dato-DXd is an ADC comprised of a humanised anti-TROP2 monoclonal antibody attached to a potent topoisomerase I inhibitor via a plasma-stable, tumour-selective cleavable linker. Dato-DXd has demonstrated activity in several tumour types, including HR+/HER2− breast cancer and TNBC.

• The results reported in Chinese patients in TROPION-PanTumor02 are comparable with those reported in the TROPION-PanTumor01 study, which was conducted in patients with advanced TNBC from the United States and Japan only.

sec.title: What is the implication, and what should change now?
sec.p: • The findings from TROPION-PanTumor02 support the investigation of Dato-DXd in patients with locally advanced or metastatic TNBC.
• Phase III studies of Dato-DXd alone or in combination in early-stage and advanced TNBC are ongoing.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Although triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) accounts for approximately 10–20% of global breast cancer diagnoses (1,2), it has an aggressive clinical course and has the highest mortality rate amongst all types of breast cancer (1-3). Single-agent chemotherapy, with or without anti-programmed cell death (ligand)-1 [PD-(L)1] immunotherapy, is the standard of care for first-line treatment of patients with metastatic TNBC without germline BRCA1/2 mutations (4). Until recently, chemotherapy was the only treatment option for patients who progressed on first-line treatment and survival outcomes were poor (4-6).

In 2021, the trophoblast cell surface antigen 2 (TROP2)-directed antibody-drug conjugate (ADC), sacituzumab govitecan, was approved in the United States and European Union as an alternative treatment option in the second-line or later based on results from the phase III ASCENT study (NCT02574455) (7-9). In ASCENT, sacituzumab govitecan demonstrated significantly improved progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) versus single-agent chemotherapy {median PFS: 5.6 vs. 1.7 months; hazard ratio (HR) 0.41 [95% confidence interval (CI): 0.32–0.52]; P<0.001; median OS: 12.1 vs. 6.7 months; HR 0.49 (95% CI: 0.38–0.59); P<0.001} and objective response rates (ORRs) of 35% and 5%, respectively, in patients with previously-treated metastatic TNBC (9). Sacituzumab govitecan was subsequently approved by China’s National Medical Products Administration (NMPA) for patients with locally advanced or metastatic TNBC who had received >2 prior systemic therapies, including at least 1 for metastatic disease (10), based on the results of the phase IIb, single-arm EVER-132-001 study (NCT04454437) which enrolled Chinese patients only (11). The results from EVER-132-001 were consistent with that of the ASCENT study; median PFS was 5.6 months and the ORR was 38.8% (OS was not evaluable at the data cutoff) (11,12). Sacituzumab tirumotecan (Sac-TMT), another TROP2-directed ADC, was approved by the NMPA in the same disease setting following data from the phase III OptiTROP-Breast01 study, which was conducted in China and demonstrated a statistically significant improvement in PFS and OS compared with chemotherapy (13). The safety profiles observed with sacituzumab govitecan and Sac-TMT were generally manageable. However, the incidence of grade III/IV treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) was higher with sacituzumab govitecan compared with chemotherapy (64% and 47%, respectively) in the ASCENT study (9). In the EVER-132-001 study, the incidence of grade ≥ III TRAEs was 71.3% (11). Rates of grade III/IV TRAEs in the OptiTROP-Breast01 study were 63.1% with Sac-TMT compared with 56.8% with chemotherapy (13). Therefore, there remains an unmet need for efficacious treatment options with manageable safety profiles for patients with TNBC who have progressed on first-line treatment.

Datopotamab deruxtecan (Dato-DXd) is an ADC comprised of a humanised anti-TROP2 immunoglobulin G1 monoclonal antibody conjugated to a highly potent topoisomerase I (Topo-I) inhibitor payload, via a plasma-stable, tumour-selective cleavable linker (14). Dato-DXd demonstrated promising clinical activity in the phase I TROPION-PanTumor01 study (NCT03401385) in patients with advanced or metastatic TNBC; the ORR was 31.8% and median PFS and OS were 4.4 months and 13.5 months, respectively (15). Dato-DXd had a manageable toxicity profile, with the most common TRAEs being low-grade stomatitis, nausea, and alopecia. In the phase III TROPION-Breast01 study (NCT05104866) in patients with previously treated inoperable or metastatic hormone receptor-positive, human epidermal growth factor receptor 2-negative (HR+/HER2−) breast cancer, Dato-DXd significantly improved the dual primary endpoint of PFS by blinded independent central review (ICR), compared with investigator’s choice of chemotherapy (ICC) [median PFS: 6.9 vs. 4.9 months; HR 0.63 (95% CI: 0.52–0.76); P<0.0001] (16); the other primary endpoint of OS did not achieve statistical significance (17). Based on the results in TROPION-Breast01, Dato-DXd has subsequently received approvals in this setting (18,19).

TROPION-PanTumor01 was conducted in patients from the United States and Japan only and did not enrol any patients from China. Therefore, in order to investigate the efficacy and safety of Dato-DXd in a Chinese population, the phase I/II TROPION-PanTumor02 study was initiated. Here we present the results of the population of patients with locally advanced or metastatic TNBC. We present this article in accordance with the TREND reporting checklist (available at https://tbcr.amegroups.com/article/view/10.21037/tbcr-2025-1-81/rc).

sec.title: Study design and patients
sec.p: TROPION-PanTumor02 (NCT05460273) is an ongoing phase I/II, multicentre, open-label, multiple-cohort study evaluating the efficacy, safety, pharmacokinetics (PK), and immunogenicity of Dato-DXd in adult Chinese patients with advanced or metastatic solid tumours. The TNBC cohort included Chinese patients (≥18 years) with inoperable locally advanced or metastatic TNBC (defined as oestrogen and progesterone receptors on <1% of tumour cells by immunohistochemistry, and HER2− per American Society of Clinical Oncology - College of American Pathologists guidelines) (20), Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status of 0 or 1, and a measurable lesion per Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumours version 1.1 (RECIST 1.1). Patients had received at least 2 prior lines of chemotherapy for advanced breast cancer, and a taxane in any setting. Poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors given to patients with germline BRCA1/2 mutations could be counted as one of the 2 prior chemotherapies. (Neo)adjuvant therapy was considered as a prior chemotherapy regimen if patients had progressed during neoadjuvant treatment, or within 12 months of completion of (neo)adjuvant therapy. Targeted agents, such as PD-(L)1 inhibitors, on their own were not counted as a prior chemotherapy regimen; however, anti-PD-(L)1 in combination with chemotherapy was counted. Prior treatment (including ADCs) with a TROP2-directed therapy or Topo-I inhibitors, or prior exposure to chemotherapy, immunotherapy, retinoid therapy, or antibody-based therapy without an adequate treatment washout period prior to enrolment was not permitted. Enrolled patients were required to have either an archival or fresh formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tumour sample to determine TROP2 expression (by central testing). Exclusion criteria included a history of another primary malignancy, persistent toxicities caused by a previous anticancer therapy, clinically significant corneal disease, previous or current brain metastasis, and history of, current, or suspected interstitial lung disease (ILD)/pneumonitis.

sec.title: Study treatment
sec.p: Patients received Dato-DXd 6 mg/kg via intravenous infusion every 3 weeks (Q3W). This dose was selected based on the results of the first-in-human phase I TROPION-PanTumor01 study (21). Treatment with Dato-DXd continued until radiological progression by investigator assessment per RECIST 1.1, unacceptable toxicity, patient’s decision to withdraw, or until other discontinuation criteria were met.

sec.title: Study endpoints and assessments
sec.p: The primary endpoint was ORR, defined as the proportion of patients with confirmed complete response (CR) or partial response (PR) by ICR per RECIST 1.1. Secondary endpoints included confirmed ORR by investigator assessment per RECIST 1.1, duration of response (DoR), disease control rate (DCR), best overall response, time to response, PFS by ICR and investigator assessment per RECIST 1.1, and OS. Safety and tolerability, and PK and immunogenicity of Dato-DXd were also assessed as secondary endpoints.

Tumour assessments were performed at baseline and every 6 weeks from day 1, cycle 1 until radiological progression by investigator assessment per RECIST 1.1. One additional follow-up was performed at the next scheduled imaging visit and no less than 4 weeks after disease progression. Survival assessments were conducted every 3 months following objective disease progression or treatment discontinuation, until death, withdrawal of consent, or the end of the study.

Safety and tolerability were assessed from screening up to 35 days after the last dose of the study drug. Adverse events (AEs) were graded according to the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) 5.0. AEs related to Dato-DXd were managed according to Dato-DXd toxicity management guidelines. All cases of potential ILD/pneumonitis were reviewed by an independent ILD adjudication committee to confirm the diagnosis and to assess whether it was related to Dato-DXd. Ophthalmologic assessments were conducted at screening, as clinically indicated during the study, and at the end of treatment; the daily use of artificial tears and avoiding the use of contact lenses was recommended. As part of an oral care plan provided to patients before study drug initiation, the daily use of prophylactic steroid-containing mouthwash was highly recommended; prophylactic cryotherapy was also suggested.

For PK analysis, blood samples were collected for the measurement of plasma concentrations of Dato-DXd, total anti-TROP2 antibody, and DXd and for the determination of anti-drug antibody (ADA). Pre- and post-dose samples for PK analysis were taken on day 1 of cycle 1, 2 (pre-dose only), 4, and 8. In the intensive sampling cohort, additional post-dose samples were taken on day 1, 2, 8, and 15 of cycle 1. PK parameters were assessed using non-compartmental analysis methods. For immunogenicity testing, pre-dose samples were taken on day 1 of cycle 1, 2, 4, and 8, and every 4 cycles thereafter; post-dose samples were taken at end of treatment and at the safety follow-up visit.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: The primary endpoint of ORR by ICR was assessed in the response evaluable set (RES), which consisted of patients who received at least one dose of study treatment and had measurable disease at baseline by ICR. PFS, OS, and safety analyses were assessed in the full analysis set (FAS), which included all patients who received at least 1 dose of treatment. PK analyses were assessed in the PK analysis set, consisting of enrolled patients who received at least 1 dose of study treatment and who had measurable plasma Dato-DXd concentrations; immunogenicity was assessed in the ADA-evaluable analysis set, consisting of those in the FAS with a result for ADAs against Dato-DXd at baseline and at least 1 post-baseline result, respectively.

Descriptive statistics were used for all variables. ORR was estimated with a two-sided 95% exact CI using the Clopper-Pearson method. Survival rates were estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method, with medians and corresponding 95% CIs estimated using the Brookmeyer-Crowley method with log-log transformation.

Approximately 78 patients were planned to be enrolled. This assumed a true ORR of 40% (31/78) and ensured an 80% probability that the lower bound of the two-sided 95% CI for ICR-assessed ORR would be greater than 25%.

sec.title: Ethical consideration
sec.p: The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and its subsequent amendments, as well as the International Conference on Harmonisation Good Clinical Practice guidelines and other applicable regulatory requirements. The study was approved by the institutional review board or ethics board at each investigational site before initiation, including of The Fifth Medical Center of the Chinese People’s Liberation Army General Hospital (No. 2022-2-9-2) and informed consent was obtained from all individual participants. This trial was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05460273).

sec.title: Patients
sec.p: A total of 79 patients were enrolled and treated. Patients had a median age of 50.0 years (range, 33–73 years) and the majority of patients had metastatic disease [n=74 (93.7%)]; visceral metastasis was reported in 63 patients (79.7%) and liver metastasis in 33 patients (41.8%) (Table 1). The representativeness of the study population is presented in Table S1. Patients had received a median of 3 prior lines of chemotherapy (range, 2‒8) in the advanced setting; 21 patients (26.6%) had received ≥5 lines. At data cutoff (6 May 2024), 5 patients (6.3%) were still receiving treatment. Of the 74 patients (93.7%) who discontinued treatment, the majority were due to disease progression [n=62 (78.5%)]. Other reasons for discontinuation were patient withdrawal [n=5 (6.3%)], subjective disease progression [n=3 (3.8%)], AEs [n=2 (2.5%)], investigator decision [n=1 (1.3%)], and starting an alternative anticancer therapy [n=1 (1.3%)]. Median duration of follow-up was 12.0 months (range, 1.3–21.6 months) and median duration of treatment was 4.5 months (range, 0.7–20.8 months).

sec.title: Efficacy
sec.p: In the RES (n=77), the confirmed ORR by ICR was 33.8% (26/77; 95% CI: 23.4–45.4%), all of whom had PRs (Table 2). In a post-hoc subgroup analysis, ORR was generally consistent across subgroups (Figure 1). Patients with a disease-free interval of >12 months had a numerically higher ORR (40.9%) compared with those who had disease-free intervals of ≤12 months (25.0%) and those who had de novo advanced disease (23.8%), although 95% CIs were overlapping across all three groups. Patients who had visceral and/or liver metastases had a numerically lower ORR (30.2% and 21.2%, respectively) compared with those who did not (50.0% and 43.2%, respectively). Those who had received <5 prior lines of chemotherapy responded better than those who had received ≥5 (36.8% vs. 25.0%). However, 95% CIs largely overlapped in each instance. Best percentage change from baseline in target lesion size, assessed by ICR per RECIST 1.1, is shown in Figure 2A. Median time to response was 1.5 months [interquartile range (IQR), 1.3–2.8] and median DoR was 6.7 months (95% CI: 4.5–12.6; Table 2); response rates at 6 and 9 months were 50.3% and 39.2%, respectively. DCR by ICR was 72.7% (56/77; 95% CI: 61.4–82.3%). ORR as assessed by the investigator was 31.2% (24/77; 95% CI: 21.1–42.7%), all of which were PRs, and median DoR was 5.8 months (95% CI: 4.0–8.4). Median time to response by investigator was 1.4 months (IQR, 1.4–1.6 months).

sec.p: In the FAS (N=79), the median PFS by ICR was 5.3 months (95% CI: 4.2–6.9). PFS rates at 6 and 12 months were 40.6% (95% CI: 29.5–51.5%) and 21.6% (95% CI: 12.1–33.0%), respectively (Figure 2B). The median OS was 13.5 months [95% CI: 10.7–not calculable (NC)] and the 6 and 12 OS rates were 83.5% (95% CI: 73.3–90.1%) and 56.9% (95% CI: 45.0–67.2%), respectively (Figure 2C).

sec.title: Safety
sec.p: A safety summary is provided in Table 3. Overall, 77 patients (97.5%) and 31 patients (39.2%) experienced treatment-emergent AEs (TEAEs) of any grade and grade ≥ III, respectively. TEAEs led to reduction, interruption, and discontinuation of Dato-DXd in 17.7%, 34.2%, and 2.5% of patients, respectively. TRAEs of any grade and grade ≥ III occurred in 75 patients (94.9%) and 25 patients (31.6%), respectively. No fatal AEs were reported.

sec.p: The most common TEAEs and TRAEs (any grade, grade ≥ III) were stomatitis (both 49.4%, 6.3%), nausea (both 43.0%, 1.3%; Table 4). The most common grade ≥ III TEAEs were hypokalaemia (7.6%) and stomatitis (6.3%; Table S2). Ocular surface events (OSEs) were observed in 12 patients (15.2%), of which 1 (1.3%) was grade ≥ III (Table 3; Table S3). The most common OSEs were corneal epithelium defect (5.1%) and dry eye (5.1%). Any grade treatment-emergent oral mucositis/stomatitis was reported in 53 patients (67.1%); 6 patients (7.6%) had grade ≥ III. Adjudicated drug-related ILD was reported in 1 patient (grade II). No patients discontinued due to adjudicated drug-related ILD, OSEs, or oral mucositis/stomatitis.

sec.title: PK and immunogenicity
sec.p: Following an intravenous dose of Dato-DXd in cycle 1, the plasma concentration-time curve of Dato-DXd and total anti-TROP2 antibody were similar. The exposure to DXd was lower than that of Dato-DXd or total anti-TROP2 antibody (Figure S1). PK profiles of Dato-DXd and total anti-TROP2 antibody were also similar. The mean half-life (± standard deviation) of Dato-DXd was 4.377 (±0.94) days (Table S4), anti-TROP2 antibody was 4.594 (±1.08) days and DXd was 5.150 (±0.92) days.

Among the 75 patients evaluable for ADA against Dato-DXd, treatment-emergent ADA-positivity, defined as treatment-boosted or treatment-induced ADA-positivity, was reported in 17 patients (22.7%). In addition, 3 patients (4.0%) were positive for neutralising antibodies. The safety profile was comparable across patients regardless of ADA status. ADA status had no significant impact on efficacy outcomes or the PK profile of Dato-DXd.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The Chinese patients with locally advanced or metastatic TNBC who received Dato-DXd in the TROPION-PanTumor02 study were heavily pretreated (patients had a median of 3 prior lines of chemotherapy in the advanced setting and 26.6% of patients had received at least 5 prior lines), and a substantial proportion of patients (41.8%) had liver metastases at baseline, both of which are associated with poor prognosis (22,23). Overall, the confirmed ORR by ICR was 33.8% (95% CI: 23.4–45.4%) and responses were durable [median DoR, 6.7 months (95% CI: 4.5–12.6)]. Response rates were generally consistent across subgroups analysed, although these exploratory results should be interpreted with caution given the small patient numbers and wide 95% CIs. Median PFS and OS were 5.3 months (95% CI: 4.2–6.9) and 13.5 months (95% CI: 10.7–NC), respectively. The efficacy of Dato-DXd reported in this study is comparable with the findings from the TROPION-PanTumor01 study, which was conducted in the United States and Japan (15). Among the 44 patients with advanced or metastatic TNBC in TROPION-PanTumor01, the ORR by blinded ICR was 31.8% (95% CI: 18.6–47.6%), although a longer median DoR of 16.8 (95% CI: 4.4–not evaluable) months was observed. Median PFS and OS were 4.4 months (95% CI: 3.0–7.3) and 13.5 months (95% CI: 10.1–16.3), respectively, similar to the results presented in this manuscript (15). Although cross-study comparisons cannot be made directly due to differences in study design, patient population, and drug payloads, these results are also broadly consistent with the efficacy of other TROP2-directed ADCs in similar treatment settings. For example, patients in the ASCENT and EVER-132-001 studies were also heavily pretreated (with a median number of 3 and 4 previous anticancer regimens, respectively) and a substantial proportion of patients (42% and 30%) had liver metastases; ORRs in the sacituzumab govitecan treatment arms were 35% and 39%, respectively (9,11). In the OptiTROP-Breast01 study, 12.3% of patients treated with Sac-TMT had received at least 3 previous lines of chemotherapy in the advanced setting, and 34.6% of patients had liver metastases; Sac-TMT demonstrated an ORR of 45.4% (13).

The safety profile observed in this study was also broadly comparable with that seen in patients with advanced TNBC in TROPION-PanTumor01 (15); low incidences of grade ≥ III TRAEs (25.0% and 31.6% in TROPION-PanTumor01 and TROPION-PanTumor02, respectively), few treatment discontinuations, and no drug-related deaths were reported. Stomatitis and nausea were the most common TRAEs in patients with advanced TNBC in both studies. Although the rates of stomatitis were lower in TROPION-PanTumor02 (49.4% compared with 72.7% in TROPION-PanTumor01), rates of the grouped-term oral mucositis/stomatitis were more similar between the two populations (67.1% and 79.5%) (15). OSEs were reported in 15.2% of patients in TROPION-PanTumor02, lower than the 36.4% of patients with TNBC with OSEs in TROPION-PanTumor01. AEs of special interest in TROPION-PanTumor02 were managed according to Dato-DXd toxicity management guidelines, which were developed based on previous clinical trial experience (16,24). In the phase III TROPION-Breast01 study in patients with previously-treated inoperable or metastatic HR+/HER2− breast cancer, Dato-DXd demonstrated a manageable safety profile compared with ICC; the incidence of grade ≥ III TRAEs was low (20.8% with Dato-DXd vs. 44.7% with ICC), there were few dose discontinuations (2.5% and 2.6%, respectively), and most AEs of special interest were low grade (16). Overall, the safety profile observed in TROPION-PanTumor02 is consistent with that seen across previously published studies of Dato-DXd in the advanced breast cancer setting.

The 6 mg/kg Dato-DXd intravenous dose given Q3W in this study was based on findings from the dose escalation and expansion phases in TROPION-PanTumor01, in patients with non-small-cell lung cancer (25), where Dato-DXd was given at doses of up to 10 mg/kg, with 6 mg/kg demonstrating an optimal benefit-risk ratio with an acceptable safety profile. Furthermore, in the TROPION-Breast01 study, patients with HR+/HER2− breast cancer received Dato-DXd 6 mg/kg; and it has since been approved in this setting (18,19). In TROPION-PanTumor02, Dato-DXd 6 mg/kg showed promising efficacy and manageable safety in Chinese patients. These results, together with findings from TROPION-PanTumor01 and TROPION-Breast01, support the use of 6 mg/kg dosing of Dato-DXd in patients with TNBC.

TROPION-PanTumor02 has some limitations, including being an early phase study with no randomisation, blinding, or comparator arm; the relatively small number of patients in the FAS (N=79) might not reflect the larger Chinese and extended Asian population, and direct comparison or extrapolations should be done with caution. In addition, this study did not include health-related quality of life assessments, which may limit the interpretation of the impact of treatment on patient-reported symptoms, functioning, and other health-related quality of life measures. Finally, existing data indicate that resistance to ADCs may involve diverse mechanisms including changes in the expression of the target antigen and evasion of payload-induced cytotoxicity (26-28), and ADCs sharing the same target antigen or similar payload may exhibit non-overlapping mechanisms of resistance (29). Further studies will be necessary to understand how combination strategies and/or ADC sequencing may overcome resistance and optimise treatment strategies.

Phase III studies of Dato-DXd alone or in combination in TNBC settings are ongoing. In the recently reported global TROPION-Breast02 study (NCT05374512), first-line Dato-DXd demonstrated statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvements in OS [median 23.7 vs. 18.7 months; HR 0.79 (95% CI: 0.64–0.98); P=0.0291] and PFS by blinded ICR [median 10.8 vs. 5.6 months; HR 0.57 (95% CI: 0.47–0.69); P<0.001] compared with chemotherapy in patients with locally recurrent inoperable or metastatic TNBC for whom immunotherapy was not an option (30). The ORR with Dato-DXd was more than double that with chemotherapy (62.5% vs. 29.3%), and safety was consistent with the known profile for Dato-DXd. In the ongoing phase III, randomised TROPION-Breast05 study (NCT06103864), Dato-DXd in combination with the immune checkpoint inhibitor durvalumab is also being investigated as first-line therapy in patients with advanced or metastatic TNBC. Studies investigating the use of Dato-DXd in combination with durvalumab in patients with earlier stages of TNBC are also underway (TROPION-Breast03: NCT05629585; TROPION-Breast04: NCT06112379).

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Dato-DXd demonstrated clinical activity and a manageable safety profile in Chinese patients with heavily pretreated locally advanced or metastatic TNBC. The findings from this study support the further investigation of Dato-DXd in patients with locally advanced or metastatic TNBC and contribute to the ongoing clinical programme investigating Dato-DXd in breast cancer.
